title: Caching
summary: A cache trades freshness for speed and reduced load by keeping a copy of data close to where it is read, and the design work is in what happens when it is stale, full, empty or down. This lesson explains the modal behaviour a cache introduces, sets out cache-aside and the other read and write patterns with the order of the write steps, compares local, shared and edge tiers, gives the time-to-live and HTTP freshness vocabulary as a table, covers eviction policies and sizing from the working set, shows how stampedes, cold starts and negative lookups are handled, and turns it into a decision per read path, with a worked sizing of a product-catalogue cache that the database can survive.

blocks.text: Facebook's memcache, as the NSDI paper describes it, is a demand-filled look-aside cache in front of MySQL: web servers read the cache, fill it on a miss, and send a delete after each database write because deletes are idempotent. Leases bound to each key stop stale sets and thundering herds, invalidations are extracted from committed SQL by the mcsqueal daemons and broadcast to every frontend cluster, servers are split into pools by churn so that cheap-to-miss keys do not evict expensive ones, and a Gutter pool of about one percent of the servers absorbs the misses of failed hosts.

blocks.text: Amazon's service teams, per the Builders' Library, justify each cache in terms of cost, latency or availability before adding it, emit hit and miss metrics and the downstream request count, use soft and hard time to live values so that a dependency brownout is survived on cached data, cache negative responses with a separate time to live, coalesce requests for uncached resources, and run load tests with caching disabled to prove the safeguards against browning out dependencies.

blocks.caption: Cloudflare's documented default edge behaviour when the origin sends no freshness headers.

blocks.text: Cloudflare's CDN caches by file extension and does not cache HTML or JSON unless a rule says so, respects private, no-store, no-cache and a zero max-age by not caching, and collapses simultaneous misses for one asset at one data centre into a single origin request with a cache lock.

Redis 6 added server-assisted client-side caching after observing that very large applications were building their own: the server tracks which keys a connection read and pushes an invalidation when one changes, with a broadcasting mode that costs no server memory, and the reference tells client authors to cap local memory, put a maximum time to live on every entry and flush the local cache when the invalidation connection is lost.

subtopics.title: What a cache buys, and the dependency it creates

blocks.text: A cache keeps a copy of data closer to where it is read, so that repeated reads skip the slow or expensive source. The gains are real and arrive quickly: latency drops, the source fleet shrinks, and brief downstream outages are smoothed over. Amazon's Builders' Library describes what happens next. Nobody remembers life before the cache, dependencies size themselves for the cached load, and the service has become addicted to its cache: a change in traffic, a cache-fleet failure or a cold restart sends the full read rate at a backend that can no longer take it.

The root of that risk is modal behaviour. A cached request and an uncached request follow different paths with different costs, and the system's capacity depends on the mix. The design work is therefore not in adding the cache but in deciding four things in advance: how it is filled, how it goes stale, what is evicted when it is full, and what happens when it is empty or down. Amazon's own checklist starts earlier still, with whether a cache is justified at all.

blocks.caption: When a cache fits, from the Amazon and Azure guidance.
rows: the same downstream result serves many requests
each request needs a unique query; the hit rate would be negligible
data that changes faster than any tolerable staleness
the service and its clients can act on an older value
a decision or a payment depends on the current value
slow, expensive to scale, or throttling on hot keys
data safe to hold in a shared store
secrets or personal data that must come from the primary source

blocks.text: Two facts about caches are easy to forget. The first is that a cache is not the source of truth: the Azure guidance and the Facebook paper both treat the cache as a store that may evict or lose anything at any time, with every important change written to the persistent store first. The second is that hit ratio is a property of the workload, not of the cache: a skewed access pattern makes a small cache valuable, and a flat one makes any cache useless.

Before adding a cache, write down the measured problem it solves, the hit ratio you expect from the access pattern, and the staleness each cached object may show. Then size the backend for the cache being empty, or decide what you will shed when it is.

subtopics.title: Cache-aside and the other read and write patterns

blocks.text: Cache-aside, also called look-aside or demand-filled, is the pattern most services start with and the one Facebook's memcache runs at a billion requests a second. The application owns the logic. On a read it asks the cache first; on a miss it reads the source, stores the result in the cache and returns it. On a write it updates the source and then deletes the cached key, so the next read repopulates it. The Facebook paper gives the reason for deleting rather than updating in one line: deletes are idempotent, so reordered or repeated invalidations cannot leave an old value behind.

blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A[Request] --> B{Key in cache?}
    B -- hit --> C[Return cached value]
    B -- miss --> D[Read from database]
    D --> E[Set key with TTL plus jitter]
    E --> C
    W[Write request] --> X[Update database]
    X --> Y[Delete cache key]
blocks.legend: Cache-aside: reads fill the cache on a miss; writes go to the source and then delete the key.

blocks.text: The order of the two write steps matters. Azure's pattern page says to update the store before removing the cached item: if the key is deleted first, a concurrent reader can miss, fetch the old row and put it back, and the cache now holds stale data until the time to live rescues it. Even in the right order a slow reader can overwrite an invalidation with a value it read before the write, which is why a time to live stays on every entry as the backstop, and why Facebook attaches a lease token to each miss so that a set with an invalidated token is refused.

the write returns after both succeed
slower writes; caches data that may never be read

blocks.text: Amazon's distinction between side caches and inline caches is the one to keep. A side cache such as Memcached or Redis is a generic store the code manipulates around its data calls; an inline cache such as an HTTP proxy or DAX hides itself behind the data API, which removes a class of bugs from application code but also removes the application's chance to compensate when the cache fleet is unavailable.

Write-through does not make the cache the source of truth; it only makes it fresh. The persistent store still takes every write, or the design has quietly moved its data into a component built to evict it.

The same object can be cached in three places, and each place changes what consistency and what failure look like. An in-process cache is a hash table in the service's own memory: no network hop, no new fleet, and the Builders' Library notes it is usually the first thing tried. Its costs follow from being private to one server. The copy on each server is different, so a client can see newer data on one call and older on the next; the downstream load is proportional to the fleet size; and a new server starts empty, so a deploy is a fleet-wide cold start.

An external cache such as Memcached or Redis gives every server the same copy, survives deploys with its data intact, offers far more memory, and makes downstream load independent of fleet size. In exchange it is another fleet to operate, with its own availability, often lower than the service it protects, and a network round trip on every read. The Azure guidance's answer to its outage is the layered design: a small local cache in front of the shared cache in front of the store, so that losing the shared tier degrades hit rate instead of availability. Amazon's teams either do that or cap the request rate to the dependency with load shedding, and test with the cache disabled.

blocks.caption: The three tiers side by side.
rows: one round trip inside the datacenter
one copy, one place to invalidate
every server misses at once: shed load or fall back to the local tier
near the user; no origin round trip
per point of presence, controlled by headers
origin takes the full load; managed caches can be purged

blocks.text: HTTP caching sorts the same tiers by who may see a response: a private cache is tied to one client and may hold a personalised response, a shared cache sits between clients and the origin and must not, and the Cache-Control directive private is the switch. Managed shared caches, meaning reverse proxies and CDNs, can be purged on demand, which standard HTTP cannot express.

Redis gives the local tier a way to stay correct: with tracking enabled the server remembers which keys each connection read and pushes an invalidation when one is modified, expired or evicted. The client must still cap its memory, put a maximum time to live on every local entry, and flush if the invalidation connection drops.
Layer the tiers in order of trust: a short-lived local copy, then the shared cache, then the source. Each layer only needs to be right about its own staleness budget.

subtopics.title: Time to live, HTTP freshness and invalidation

blocks.text: A time to live bounds how old a cached value may be before the cache stops serving it; it is the simplest staleness control and the one every other mechanism falls back on. Redis attaches an expiry with EXPIRE or the EX option of SET, resolves it to the millisecond, and replicates and persists it. The number comes from the business, not from habit: too short sends reads straight back to the store, too long serves stale data, and Amazon's teams have seen outages from values picked once and never revisited.

Amazon adds two refinements. Entries created together expire together, so a random jitter on each expiry spreads the misses out. And a soft time to live that triggers a refresh attempt, separate from a hard one past which the stale value is no longer used, lets a downstream brownout be survived on cached data; the IAM client uses that pair.

blocks.caption: The HTTP freshness vocabulary, from RFC 9111, RFC 5861 and MDN.
rows: the response is stale once its age exceeds N seconds; Age carries the elapsed time through shared caches
the same limit for shared caches only, overriding max-age and Expires there
a cache may guess a lifetime from Last-Modified; the RFC suggests at most about a tenth of the interval since that time
store it, but revalidate with the origin before every reuse
do not store the request or response at all; not a privacy mechanism
only the client's own cache may store it; the switch for personalised responses
once stale, never reuse without a successful validation; a disconnected cache returns an error instead
the cache key is the URL plus the named request headers, so a language or encoding variant is stored separately
serve the stale copy for up to N seconds while revalidating in the background
serve the stale copy for up to N seconds if the origin answers with a server error

blocks.text: Validation is the second HTTP mechanism: a stale entry is checked with a conditional request carrying its ETag or Last-Modified, and a 304 Not Modified answer makes it fresh again without a body. For application caches the equivalent is explicit invalidation: delete the key when the row is written, or publish change events, as Facebook's mcsqueal daemons do by broadcasting the deletes embedded in committed SQL to every frontend cluster. Where a cache cannot be reached, change the name instead: versioned keys and cache-busting URLs put new data under a new key.

Set the time to live from the staleness the product tolerates, add jitter, invalidate on write where the tolerance is shorter than any sensible value, and keep the time to live anyway as the backstop for the invalidation that gets lost.

subtopics.title: Eviction policies and sizing the cache

blocks.text: A cache has a memory limit, and the eviction policy decides which keys go when it is reached. Redis sets the limit with maxmemory and the behaviour with maxmemory-policy; with no limit a 64-bit server simply grows. The policies differ in two ways: which keys are candidates, every key or only those with an expiry set, and how a candidate is chosen, by recency, by frequency, by time to live or at random. Redis approximates recency and frequency by sampling a few keys rather than keeping an exact list, because an exact list costs memory; under a power-law access pattern the difference is minimal.

blocks.caption: The Redis maxmemory policies and when each fits.
rows: the instance holds durable data; the default when nothing is set
a subset of keys is accessed far more than the rest; the documentation's default choice for a cache
least frequently used, with a decaying counter
frequency predicts reuse better than recency
keys are accessed with roughly equal frequency, as in a repeating cycle
one instance holds both cache and persistent keys; the documentation suggests two instances instead
the shortest remaining time to live
the code can mark good eviction candidates with short expiries

blocks.text: LRU is the default because it is simple and good enough for skewed workloads, but it has a known failure: a scan of many keys read once evicts the whole working set. The Caffeine library's evaluation against real traces shows the alternatives, ARC, LIRS and Window TinyLFU, all beating LRU, and chose Window TinyLFU because it reaches a near-optimal hit rate with a frequency sketch of a few bits per entry, admitting a new key only when it is likely to be used more than the key it would evict.

Sizing starts from the working set, not the data set. Access is skewed, so a fraction of the keys serves most reads; estimate the hot entries, multiply by the average value size plus per-key overhead, and validate against production, because real traffic differs from the model. Redis exposes the measurement directly: keyspace hits over hits plus misses is the hit ratio, a high evicted-keys count says the cache is too small or the policy wrong, and a high expired-keys count says the time to live is too short. Facebook found that keys with different churn interfere, valuable slow-changing keys being evicted before dead fast-changing ones, and split its servers into pools by churn and miss cost.
Never run an allkeys policy on an instance that also holds data the application cannot recreate: eviction will delete it silently. The cache and the durable keys belong on different instances.

subtopics.title: Stampedes, cold starts and the cache as a failure mode

blocks.text: The failures a cache introduces are all the same event at different scales. A thundering herd is many requests missing the same key at once, each recomputing the value and hitting the backend; Facebook's paper names the common trigger, a key under heavy read and write where each write invalidates the entry and sends the next wave of reads to the database. A cold start is the same miss across every key after a restart, a flush or a new server joining the fleet. A negative lookup, a key that does not exist, misses every time unless the absence itself is cached.

The remedy for the herd is to let one caller fill the key while the others wait or take the old value. Amazon calls it request coalescing, HTTP caches call it request collapsing, and Cloudflare implements it as a cache lock: one request per asset per data centre goes to the origin and the response is streamed to everyone waiting. Facebook's lease does the same at the key level, handing out one fill token per key every ten seconds and telling other missers to wait a few milliseconds and retry.

blocks.caption: Facebook's measured effect of leases on a set of keys prone to thundering herds, over one week.

blocks.text: For negative results, cache the error or the absence with its own, usually shorter, time to live; Amazon has seen failure rates rise when a service kept asking a dependency for a resource that no longer existed and discarded each error. For a cache that is down or empty, the Builders' Library is explicit that falling straight through to the dependency can turn a cache outage into a dependency outage, and prefers a local-cache fallback or a cap on the request rate to the backend. Facebook's Gutter pool, about one percent of the memcached servers, takes over for failed servers and converts a large share of would-be misses into hits within minutes.

items: Coalesce misses per key so the backend sees one fill, not a herd.
Put jitter on expiries so entries filled together do not expire together.
Cache negative results and errors with their own time to live.
Wrap cache calls in short timeouts and a circuit breaker so a slow cache does not stall every request.
Load test with the cache disabled, and make the backend's rate limit or load shedding the thing that holds in that state.

blocks.text: Design the empty-cache path first. If the backend cannot survive a flush, the mitigation is not a warmer cache but a cap on what reaches the backend.

subtopics.title: Choosing the cache for one read path

blocks.text: The choice is per read path, and it starts with whether to cache at all. The decision below applies the sources' guidance to the question a design review asks: this endpoint, this data, this staleness budget. The example column names the kind of data each option is usually right for; the cost of being wrong is the modal behaviour of the first subtopic.

blocks.caption: Picking the caching approach for one read path.

rows.pick_when: each request needs a unique result, the source is already fast, or the data is sensitive or decision-critical
rows.avoid_when: a dependency throttles on hot keys or a dashboard shows the same query answered thousands of times
rows.example: a per-user export; a balance read before a debit

rows.pick_when: a small, slow-changing set of objects, tolerant of per-server differences and of an empty cache after each deploy
rows.avoid_when: fleet size makes downstream load from cold starts dangerous, or servers must agree
rows.example: configuration, feature flags, a template; the local tier in front of a shared cache

rows.pick_when: many servers read the same objects, one place to invalidate is wanted, and a cache outage may degrade to slower reads
rows.avoid_when: the code cannot be trusted to keep the cache and store in order, or read-after-write freshness is required
rows.example: user profiles, catalogue entries, rendered fragments: the default pattern

rows.pick_when: a uniform client API matters more than the application's ability to compensate for a cache outage
rows.avoid_when: the cache fleet is less available than the dependency it fronts and no fallback exists
rows.example: an HTTP cache in front of a REST dependency; a database accelerator

rows.pick_when: a read-heavy path must show its own write immediately
rows.avoid_when: data is rarely read after it is written, or changes constantly
rows.example: a shopping cart; a user's own settings page

rows.pick_when: whole responses are reusable across users and can be keyed by URL and a few headers
rows.avoid_when: responses are personalised and cannot be marked private, or must be current on every request
rows.example: images, scripts with hashed names, public pages with a purge on change

blocks.text: Two patterns recur in the sources. The first is layering: a local tier for latency and for surviving the shared tier's outage, a shared tier for coherence, the source for truth. The second is that the invalidation path is designed with the same care as the read path: who deletes which keys on which writes, in what order, and what the time to live is for the deletes that get lost. A review that cannot answer those questions has found an eventual-consistency bug waiting to be reported.

Choose the pattern by what happens when the cache is wrong or gone, not by what happens when it hits. Cache-aside with delete-on-write and a time to live is the default because both answers are tolerable.

worked_example.title: Worked example: a product-catalogue read path from 20,000 reads per second

blocks.text: A retail service serves product pages from a catalogue in a relational database. The team must decide whether to cache, size the cache, set its time to live and invalidation, and make sure the database survives an empty cache. Every input is an assumption chosen to make the arithmetic concrete; the patterns are the cache-aside pattern, the Redis policies and the Amazon checklist.

blocks.title: From the read rate to a cache that the backend can survive
items: Reads: 20,000 product reads per second at peak (assumption), against a database load-tested at 4,000 reads per second.

Reuse: the same product is read many times, so the data is cacheable; prices change a few times a day and a one-minute delay is acceptable to the product owner (assumption), so the data tolerates staleness.
Data set: 2 million products at about 2 kB each is 4 GB in total.
Working set: about a tenth of the products draw nine tenths of the reads (assumption from access logs), so 200,000 hot entries at 2 kB is 400 MB.
Memory: with per-key overhead and headroom the cache is sized at 1 GB, under an allkeys-lru policy because a skewed subset is read far more than the rest.
Hit ratio: holding the whole working set gives about 90 percent hits, so misses at peak are about 2,000 per second, half of what the database sustains.
Time to live: 60 seconds plus up to 10 seconds of jitter, because invalidation on write handles price changes and the time to live only catches lost deletes.
Invalidation: a price or stock change updates the row and then deletes the product's key; the next read refills it.
Negative lookups: a missing product id is cached as absent for 30 seconds so that crawlers hitting dead ids do not reach the database.
Hot key: a featured product at 2,000 reads per second expires once a minute; misses for that key are coalesced so the database sees one fill per expiry.
Empty cache: 20,000 reads per second would reach a database sized for 4,000, so the service caps database reads at 3,500 per second and sheds the rest with a short retry hint until the cache refills.
The decider: the empty-cache cap, not the hit ratio. With it, a flush costs a few minutes of partial errors; without it, a flush is an outage of the database and everything behind it.

blocks.caption: The design as a reviewer should receive it: one row per quantity, with its rule.
rows: working set plus overhead and headroom
staleness budget of a minute; jitter against mass expiry
3,500 reads per second to the database

blocks.code:
import json, random

TTL, JITTER = 60, 10          # seconds; the staleness budget and the spread against mass expiry

def get_product(cache, db, product_id):
    key = f"product:{product_id}"
    hit = cache.get(key)
    if hit is not None:
        return None if hit == b"\x00" else json.loads(hit)   # the absent marker is a negative entry
    row = db.load_product(product_id)            # source of truth
    if row is None:
        cache.set(key, b"\x00", ex=30)           # negative cache, shorter TTL
        return None
    cache.set(key, json.dumps(row), ex=TTL + random.randint(0, JITTER))
    return row

def update_product(cache, db, product_id, fields):
    db.save_product(product_id, fields)           # update the store first
    cache.delete(f"product:{product_id}")        # then delete: idempotent, never overwrite
blocks.caption: Cache-aside as the example sizes it: a jittered time to live, a negative entry for missing ids, and delete-on-write in the order the pattern requires. Coalescing of misses and the empty-cache cap live in the service's request layer.
